chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Hammad ibn Isa and Ibn Abi 'Umayr from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
I asked him about the dyer and the fuller, and he said, 'They are not liable for compensation (if they damage the cloth).'

The meaning in this narration is that they are not liable if they are trustworthy; as for if they are suspected, they are liable, according to what we have previously mentioned in the narration of Abu Basir and others.

key_terms.اتَّهَمَهُمَا: Suspected them / Accused them of negligence
key_terms.وَالْقَصَّارُ: And the fuller (one who cleans and thickens wool/cloth)
key_terms.يُضَمَّنَانِ: They are made liable / They bear compensation

ai.seo_question: Are dyers and fullers liable for damage to clothes if they are trustworthy?
ai.summary: In *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Shaykh al-Tusi records this narration from Imam al-Sadi’ (AS) to clarify the principle of *al-amanah* (trustworthiness) in artisan contracts, distinguishing between the *dhimmah* (inherent liability) of trustworthy (*ma'mun*) workers and those who are suspected (*muttaham*). This ruling underscores the Shia juristic emphasis on the worker's character as a determinant of liability, aligning with the broader legal theory that a trustworthy agent is not liable for minor negligence unless specified. The context highlights the practical application of trust in commercial transactions within the early Shia community.
